summary:
The Further Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2024, Public Law 118-47, provides further consolidated appropriations for fiscal year 2024, ending September 30, 2024, and includes related policy provisions and amendments to existing law. It covers the Departments of Defense, Treasury, Homeland Security, Labor, Health and Human Services, Education, State, foreign operations, the legislative branch, and related agencies. References to “this Act” generally apply only within each division, and the explanatory statement printed in the Congressional Record is given effect for allocations and related purposes.

For the Department of Defense, the Act funds military personnel, operations and maintenance, procurement, research and development, revolving funds, and related agencies, and imposes numerous conditions. It restricts certain housing repair funds, requires notice for defense innovation projects over $5,000,000, preserves National Intelligence Program budget structures, and provides $100,000,000 for AFRICOM and SOUTHCOM partner capacity. It provides $500,000,000 for Israeli cooperative missile defense programs, including Iron Dome, Arrow, and short-range ballistic missile defense, and $1,290,093,000 for prior-year Navy shipbuilding cost increases. It bars nuclear-armed missile-defense interceptors and decommissioning of specified ships, and permits up to $20,000,000 in Navy transfers for shipbuilding inflation through September 30, 2028.

The financial services and general government division funds Treasury, the Executive Office of the President, the Judiciary, the District of Columbia, independent agencies, and government-wide requirements. It provides, among other amounts, $78,904,000 for White House operations, $129,000,000 for OMB, and $298,579,000 through September 30, 2025, for High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas. It restricts FCC changes to certain universal service high-cost support rules, requires pornography blocking on federally funded computer networks with law-enforcement exceptions, sets conference and travel restrictions, provides $2,850,000 for the Inspectors General Council Fund, and bars SEC rules requiring disclosure of political contributions or trade association dues. It rescinds $10,200,000,000 from an Inflation Reduction Act account, $1,768,000,000 from an American Rescue Plan account, and other unobligated balances. Government-wide provisions address drug-free workplaces, vehicle purchase caps, citizenship conditions for pay, whistleblower protections, contractor tax and felony restrictions, conference reporting, and limits on certain political disclosure requirements.

The Homeland Security division funds DHS components, including $2,382,814,000 for CISA operations and support, $489,401,000 for CISA procurement and construction, $1,483,990,000 for FEMA operations and support, and $3,497,019,369 for FEMA federal assistance. FEMA assistance includes State Homeland Security Grants, Urban Area Security Initiative grants, nonprofit security grants, firefighter assistance and SAFER grants totaling $648,000,000, emergency management grants, flood mapping, emergency food and shelter, and community project and congressionally directed spending. Secret Service provisions allow reimbursable training obligations, restrict protection of other agency heads except by reimbursement, and permit limited reprogramming.

The Labor-HHS-Education division funds labor, health, and education programs and changes several laws. Labor provisions allow limited transfers for technical assistance, program integrity, and evaluation; create a temporary Fair Labor Standards Act overtime exemption for disaster claims adjusters; modify H-2B seafood worker entry and prevailing wage rules; restrict enforcement of certain H-2B regulations; authorize a Labor Secretary security detail; and allow disposition of specified Job Corps properties. It rescinds $206,000,000 from an immigration-related account and $75,000,000 from fiscal 2023 training funds. HHS provisions include major HRSA funding, alter Head Start eligibility rules for tribal and migrant/seasonal programs beginning in fiscal 2024 and thereafter, rescind $1,250,000,000 from the HHS Nonrecurring Expenses Fund, and rescind $70,000,000 from child welfare incentive balances. Education funding includes $19,107,790,000 for Education for the Disadvantaged, $1,625,151,000 for Impact Aid, $5,776,178,000 for School Improvement, $194,746,000 for Indian Education, and $1,115,000,000 for Innovation and Improvement, with specified availability dates and program allocations.

The Legislative Branch division funds congressional operations and support agencies. It requires minimization procedures when federal entities assist House cybersecurity. It funds the Capitol Police at $588,627,000 for salaries and $202,846,000 for general expenses, CBO at $70,000,000, the Joint Committee on Taxation at $13,554,000, the Office of Congressional Workplace Rights at $8,150,000, and numerous Architect of the Capitol accounts, including major building, grounds, power plant, security, and renovation projects.

The State and foreign operations division funds diplomacy, foreign assistance, international organizations, and development finance. It appropriates $983,250,000 for the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, with a $12,000,000,000 cap on total loan and guaranteed principal, and $87,000,000 for the Trade and Development Agency. It imposes reporting, consultation, and facility-security requirements, withholds $100,000,000 in Diplomatic Programs funds pending embassy security guidance, and bars moving the U.S. embassy in Israel outside Jerusalem. It extends Afghan special immigrant visa authority, raising the cap to 50,500 and extending deadlines to December 31, 2025, and January 31, 2026. It provides up to $125,000,000 for contingencies, sets Ukraine oversight and reporting conditions, caps certain contributions to Ukraine unless waived, provides at least $300,000,000 for countering Russian influence, restricts assistance involving Russia and occupied territories, and conditions or bars funding for certain U.N. bodies.

The Act also includes an “Other Matters” division addressing extensions and other matters, Udall Foundation reauthorization, a funding limitation for the United Nations Relief and Works Agency, and budgetary effects.
